take_homes: A standard of 'good' has two parts: one that stops errors and one that raises quality. Written down, it can be applied when I am not in the room.
A measure has to be tested by comparing it with human judgment, and a flat score may mean the measure is exhausted, not that the work is done.
My role moves from checking each output to owning the standard and the process. I must decide which categories never go without a human, and keep reading real output myself so I don't lose the eye.

monday.move: Ask the DPO and a works-council representative what is allowed before I put any employee data into an agent. In parallel, sit down with one HR partner and write on paper what 'good' means for my weekly people-metrics summary: what it must never get wrong, and what would make a leader act on it. No tool involved yet.
monday.who: Me, our DPO, one HR business partner, and the works council rep if the DPO says to involve them
monday.when: Ask the DPO Monday morning. Hold the 45-minute session with the HR partner by Thursday.
monday.stop_condition: If the DPO says personal data can't go in this tool, I use only aggregated or invented data, or I stop. I don't try the agent on real employee data.
monday.blocker: Employee data in an AI tool needs the works council and the DPO, and I haven't asked either yet.

misconception.why: The module says the human moves up to design the loop and own the standard, and some work always keeps a human. That makes me less sure headcount goes first. But it never talked about which roles shrink or how hiring changes, and it offered no evidence, so I still expect to be asked which roles go.

one_line: Useful if you want to know how to keep a standard of 'good' running without being in the room, but far too much tool detail, and nobody said a word about what it means for people's jobs.
